stories.headline: Longmont Officer Fatally Shoots Suspect During Domestic Hostage Standoff
stories.summary:
A Longmont police officer shot and killed a 20-year-old man Monday afternoon after the suspect allegedly took a victim hostage during a domestic-related disturbance near Creekside Drive and Eagle View Circle. Three officers responded around 2:30 p.m. and learned upon arrival that the suspect had seized a hostage.

During the ensuing standoff, the suspect repeatedly claimed to be armed and refused multiple commands to comply. An officer ultimately fired, and the suspect was transported to a hospital where he was pronounced dead. His identity had not been released as of Tuesday.

The officer who fired has been placed on paid administrative leave per department policy, a standard procedure following officer-involved shootings. The 20th Judicial District Critical Incident Team is conducting an independent investigation; Longmont police will not participate in the probe. Police noted the suspect was involved in a pending Boulder County case involving the same victim.

stories.headline: Colorado Confidential Informant Helped Kill Two Men After Plea Deal Freed Him, Records Show
stories.summary:
A Colorado confidential informant named Anthony Fogle was released from jail in a 2022 plea deal brokered by Fremont County detective Stephen Krueger and then-prosecutor Jeff Lindsey — and four months later allegedly participated in the kidnapping and murder of two men in a remote canyon. Rodolfo Santillan-Reyes, 36, and Ryan Roth, 25, were bound, driven up Phantom Canyon Road, shot, and kicked into a ravine. Santillan-Reyes survived long enough to drag himself under a bush before dying.

Fogle exchanged 146 texts with Detective Krueger in the three months before the killings, spoke with him by phone hours before the murders, and met with the FBI and Krueger days after. Yet his status as a confidential informant remained hidden from defense attorneys for years, violating Colorado's discovery rules.

Fremont County District Court Judge Lauren Swan sanctioned the district attorney's office in July for failing to disclose the arrangement and removed the DA's office from one suspect's case. Fogle, now 49, along with Suzzette Salyer, 44, and Toni Gurule, 45, were charged with first-degree murder in 2024. Fogle agreed to testify against the women in exchange for a plea capped at 25 years.

Lindsford, now the elected Fremont County DA, testified in July that he could not recall the specifics of the deal that freed Fogle. The detective claimed he forgot about the informant paperwork and falsely denied being in contact with Fogle around the time of the killings, according to the judge's findings.

stories.headline: More Than 200 New Colorado Laws Take Effect Wednesday, Covering Housing, Bears, Social Media and More
stories.summary:
Wednesday marks three months since the close of Colorado's 2026 legislative session, triggering the start date for more than 200 new state laws. The legislation covers a wide range of areas including affordable housing development, ride-hailing app safety, vision testing for pre-kindergarten students, and a ban on credit cards for sports betting deposits.

Among the notable measures: it is now a misdemeanor to knowingly leave food or edible trash in circumstances where it could lure a wild bear. A law named for cyclist Magnus White, killed in Boulder County in 2023, requires law enforcement to offer voluntary alcohol breath tests for drivers involved in crashes that kill or seriously injure others. New parents may now voluntarily relinquish a newborn to hospitals or emergency centers for up to 30 days without facing child abuse charges.

Senate Bill 11 requires social media platforms with more than one million monthly users to establish streamlined processes for law enforcement search warrants and comply within 72 hours. The law was passed in the wake of a 2025 shooting at Evergreen High School in Jefferson County, in which investigators said social media companies were slow to produce information about the shooter. An earlier version of the bill was vetoed by Gov. Jared Polis.

Another new law, House Bill 1110, allows Colorado banks to take protective actions when they suspect elder financial abuse or fraud. The batch of laws would have been larger were it not for Polis's record 11 vetoes during the session.

stories.headline: Colorado Economy Shows Mixed Signals at Mid-Year as Inflation Rises and Labor Force Shrinks
stories.summary:
A University of Colorado Boulder report released Tuesday found Colorado's economy continuing to expand through the first half of 2026 despite rising inflation, slowing job growth, and the economic ripple effects of elevated global oil prices tied to the U.S.-Iran conflict. The state added 28,600 jobs in June, a 1% year-over-year increase, though twelve industries posted losses compared to eight with gains. Healthcare and social assistance led growth.

Inflation in the Denver-Aurora-Lakewood metro area rose 5% over the past year as of May — the highest level since 2023 and the second-highest among 12 major U.S. metro regions, behind only Urban Hawaii. That figure outpaces the national annual average of 4.2%. Oil prices, while down 31% from their April peak, remain 16% above year-ago levels and continue to pressure consumers.

CU Boulder economists flagged stagflation risk — a combination of weak growth, rising unemployment, and persistent inflation — as a key concern, though they noted recession risks nationally are fading. Colorado's labor force shrank by nearly 65,000 people year-over-year, dropping the state to 46th nationally in rate of change. An aging population and slowing net migration are cited as driving factors.

On the positive side, Colorado recorded more than 64,000 new business filings in the second quarter of 2026, up 25% year-over-year and bucking typical seasonal declines. Economists said much of the federal-policy uncertainty that dominated 2025 has stabilized, allowing the state to navigate the period with what they characterized as 'soft growth.'

stories.headline: Reality TV Real Estate Firm Serhant Expands to Denver, Targeting Luxury Market
stories.summary:
Serhant, the luxury real estate brokerage founded by Netflix and Bravo reality television personality Ryan Serhant, announced Tuesday it is expanding to Denver, describing the move as its largest single-market entry to date. The firm has poached 11 founding agents from prominent local brokerages including Compass, Valor Real Estate, LPT Realty, and 8z Real Estate, with those agents having collectively closed more than $1 billion in sales over the past year.

The Colorado office will be led by Rebecca Ferguson, a Denver broker with more than 12 years of experience and former managing broker of Kentwood Real Estate's Cherry Creek office. Serhant said Denver's luxury market was among the most exciting in the country and that the firm's AI-driven platform, called S.MPLE, would give agents a competitive edge in marketing and transaction management.

Founded in 2020, Serhant has amassed more than 3 million Instagram followers and 1.4 million on TikTok and has been expanding westward, with launches in Arizona in 2025 and California and Texas earlier this year. The firm differentiates itself through heavy use of social media and proprietary technology for lead generation, listing presentations, and scheduling.

stories.headline: Broncos Training Camp Day 10: Center Depth at Crisis Point as Third Starter Goes Down
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos' center position reached a critical juncture during Day 10 of training camp when Michael Deiter was carted to the locker room Tuesday, following earlier absences by starters Luke Wattenberg and Alex Forsyth. Deiter had been signed in the offseason for depth after seven seasons split between Miami, Houston, and Washington. With all three centers unavailable, undrafted rookie Gavin Ortega stepped in for depth while Calvin Throckmorton assumed first-team reps.

The Broncos are approaching their preseason opener Friday and spent Tuesday's session focusing on situational football. All-Pro guard Quinn Meinerz, who has experience at center from earlier in his career, has been discussed internally as a potential emergency option, though moving one of the NFL's premier guards would be far from ideal.

Wide receiver Tez Bryant continued to stand out in camp, benefiting from additional reps while Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton have missed time. Bryant, selected with the 74th pick in the 2025 NFL Draft out of Illinois, is drawing significant attention for his performances and is seen as a potential reshaper of Denver's receiving corps.

stories.headline: Cherry Hills Village Faces Criticism for E-Bike Ban Along High Line Canal Trail
stories.summary:
Cherry Hills Village is drawing pushback from trail users after posting signs prohibiting electric bicycles along its stretch of the High Line Canal trail, one of the longest continuous urban trails in the country at 71 miles. The affluent Arapahoe County city of about 6,400 residents bans all motorized vehicles on its trails, and city officials say e-bikes fall under that prohibition because they have motors. The ban creates a discontinuity along the trail, as neighboring Greenwood Village and Denver both permit e-bikes.

Critics, including retired geriatrician Robert Schwartz, 78, argue the ban unfairly restricts older and mobility-limited residents from accessing exercise. Schwartz, a 25-year Cherry Hills Village resident, said seniors who rely on e-bikes for low-impact exercise may be deterred from riding altogether after seeing the prohibition signs. He said he has attempted to raise the issue with city officials without response.

Cherry Hills Village spokeswoman Denise White said the citywide rule reflects safety concerns on paths shared by pedestrians, cyclists, children, pets, and equestrians. The city does provide an exception for those using e-bikes for disability-related mobility assistance. E-bikes are similarly banned in Waterton Canyon at the trail's western terminus, where the U.S. Forest Service classifies the path as non-motorized.

stories.headline: Iconic DIA Murals Return to Great Hall Following Years of Construction
stories.summary:
Denver International Airport announced that artwork by muralist Leo Tanguma is returning to the Great Hall following years of construction as part of the ongoing Great Hall renovation project. The mural 'In Peace and Harmony with Nature,' depicting environmental destruction, is now back on display on Level 5 in the northwest end of the terminal.

The Great Hall Construction project began in 2018 and is expected to wrap up by the end of 2027. One of Tanguma's most recognized works, 'Children of the World Dream Peace,' featuring a soldier in a gas mask and children holding a sword, will remain in storage and is slated to return to the south end of the terminal in 2028.

Tanguma's murals have been part of DIA since the airport's opening in the 1990s and are among the most recognized and debated works of public art in Denver, frequently cited in popular discussions about the airport's distinctive character.

stories.headline: About 10 Hospitalized, Dozens Treated for Heat Illness at Colorado Springs Music Festival
stories.summary:
Approximately 10 people were hospitalized and 20 to 30 others were treated for heat-related illnesses Saturday at blocktickets PARK in Colorado Springs during the Colorado Tacos and Tequila Festival, according to Colorado Springs Fire Department spokeswoman Ashley Franco. Medical staff had been stationed at the outdoor venue since around 2 p.m., but were overwhelmed as dozens more began reporting symptoms throughout the afternoon.

The festival drew large crowds to the 8,500-capacity stadium on Tutt Boulevard for a hip-hop and R&B concert lineup featuring T.I., Ginuwine, and Chingy. Gates opened at 2 p.m., and the final performance was scheduled for 8:45 p.m. By 7:30 p.m., a total of 30 to 40 people had been affected.

The high temperature in Colorado Springs on Saturday reached 97 degrees, tying the daily record set in 2025, according to the National Weather Service in Pueblo. A heat advisory for the region had been in effect until 8 p.m. that day. The incident underscores risks associated with large outdoor events during Colorado's ongoing summer heat patterns.

stories.headline: Multiple Lawsuits Filed Over Colorado's Statewide Packaging Recycling Fee
stories.summary:
Multiple parties have filed lawsuits challenging a Colorado packaging fee designed to expand curbside-style recycling access statewide, according to the Colorado Sun. The fee, part of a broader producer responsibility initiative, was intended to shift recycling costs from local governments and taxpayers to the companies that manufacture and sell packaged goods.

The legal challenges mark a significant complication for one of Colorado's more ambitious environmental policy efforts in recent years. Details of the plaintiffs and specific legal arguments were not fully specified in available reporting, but the litigation raises questions about implementation timelines and the long-term viability of the recycling program.

Colorado has been working to expand recycling infrastructure beyond the Front Range urban core, where curbside service is widely available, to rural and smaller communities that currently lack consistent access. The outcome of the lawsuits could affect how and when that expansion proceeds.

stories.headline: Semitrailer Fire Temporarily Shuts Down Northbound I-25 Near Pueblo
stories.summary:
A semitrailer fire closed northbound Interstate 25 near Pueblo for more than an hour Tuesday morning, disrupting traffic along one of Colorado's primary north-south corridors. Colorado Department of Transportation data showed northbound lanes were closed between Exit 97A for Central Avenue and Exit 97B for Abriendo Avenue beginning at 10:30 a.m.

The highway was fully reopened by 11:50 a.m., according to Pueblo police. No injuries were reported in connection with the fire, and details on the cause of the blaze were not immediately available.

stories.headline: Denver Parents and Providers Push to Shape City's Response to Childcare Crisis
stories.summary:
Denver parents and childcare providers are raising their voices about the city's ongoing childcare affordability and availability crisis, with community input now being incorporated into policy discussions about what solutions should look like, according to Denver7. The engagement effort reflects growing pressure on city leaders to address a shortage that advocates say affects working families across income levels.

Childcare costs in the Denver metro area have risen sharply in recent years, straining household budgets and forcing some parents to reduce work hours or exit the workforce entirely. Local officials and advocacy groups have been exploring a range of interventions, including subsidies, expanded provider capacity, and workforce supports for childcare workers themselves.

topStory.headline: Houthi Missile Attack on Red Sea Cargo Ship Kills Six, Marking Deadliest Strike on Shipping Since Conflict Escalated
topStory.summary:
Iranian-backed Houthi rebels killed six people and wounded at least 10 others Tuesday after firing three ballistic missiles at a commercial cargo vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, off the southern tip of Yemen. Yemen's Transport Ministry identified the stricken ship as the Tihamah, sailing under a Tanzanian flag and owned by an Egyptian operator, which the ministry described as a Yemeni commercial vessel carrying food. Four crew members — three Pakistanis and one Indonesian — were among the dead, along with two members of Yemen's government-allied National Resistance Forces who responded to the scene.

Yemen's coast guard reported that a second missile strike targeted rescuers attempting to evacuate the burning vessel, compounding the casualties. The Houthis, for their part, claimed the ship was carrying Saudi military equipment. The attack is the first to cause confirmed fatalities from Houthi strikes on shipping since the United States and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, and it comes after the Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi ports last month.

The vessel strike is part of a broader and accelerating Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognized Yemeni government. The Houthis have also targeted the Red Sea port city of Mokha with ballistic missiles, killing at least seven people there on Sunday and striking again Monday, and have attacked Saudi oil facilities and tankers. A drone strike in Yemen's Shabwa province killed two government soldiers Monday, while tit-for-tat clashes have extended to al-Jawf, Saada, and Marib provinces.

The escalation threatens to reignite Yemen's civil war following a UN-brokered truce reached in April 2022 that had largely ended major fighting. The Houthis have controlled the capital, Sanaa, since 2014; the Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the government, which now operates from Aden. Violence resumed July 13 after a Saudi airstrike on Sanaa airport blocked an Iranian flight carrying a senior Houthi delegation, triggering retaliatory strikes that have grown into the deadliest exchange in years.

With Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupting roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments, international attention has shifted sharply to the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb strait as an alternative route for Saudi crude exports. UN envoy Hans Grundberg warned Friday that Yemen faces a greater risk of large-scale conflict than at any point since the 2022 truce, cautioning that the fighting risks drawing the country into a wider regional confrontation. Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul-Salam said the group remains open to negotiations but insisted any settlement must include lifting the Saudi-led air and sea blockade imposed in 2015.
